c: Mild disclaimer, I am the kind of person who
watches videos at 2.5x, so I will talk fast.
You can please interrupt with clarification questions. There's a decent chance that if you
have a critique of the things that I'm
saying strategy-wise, that I will address that later
in the talk. If I don't, then I'm going to
try and have lots of time for questions at the end.
But I will start by highlighting that you
could imagine three things that people have written
about at different times, either how do you
make sure that people ordering DNA sequences from
100 different companies for different parts of a
dangerous genome, or how do you actually verify
that the politician's team giving proof-of-life photos are giving real proof-of-life photos or
having agent-agent interactions where you can link the people's identity to the agents.
These are things that people can identify. They,
if done badly, or not solved at all,
will start to seriously erode infrastructure as people use AI systems more and more
often and as those systems get more capable. The general solution direction that people
often identify for something like this is let's have a
DNA or a DNS for people. The domain name
service is how your computer knows that it
is reaching the website that it thinks it is.
And there is a substantial sociotechnical amount of infrastructure behind this.
And it's really hard to just snap your fingers
and magic it into existence. But when you talk
to a lot of people around things like
biosecurity, they tend to assume this primitive already exists
or will exist in a timely manner. And if
you look at what that solution would look like,
people often either point to OAuth and like, we'll
just use login with Google, we'll use passports or
mobile driver's licenses, we'll use something like Worldcoin.
And the problems with these are that
some of them are not societally load-bearing as identification systems currently. Some of
them are poorly adopted and will be adoption
limited. And some have multiple failure modes.
And I think that it is very useful to be
able to look at these types of things and say,
what would the best solution look like if you
were handed a blank slate? Banks have already solved
all of those problems. The know-your-customer laws require that banks confirm identity in
a way that is societally load-bearing, has obvious key
recovery — you go to the bank — and
is incentive-aligned, where if someone steals your driver's license, passport, and your credit cards,
and you for some reason couldn't call the bank
to cancel your cards because they stole your phone
too, you're probably going to try to orchestrate
replacing your driver's license and passport while
in line at the bank. You want that
kind of property for your identification system. And
the question becomes, can we use this solution,
if you care about mitigating those downstream risks,
potential risks from AI. And the problem is that fixing
this, trying to get banks to expose KYC to
mobile wallets, is not anyone's job. There is no
chance this will return the fund, so no founder
should pursue it — the big companies will
eat your lunch. The researchers — the big companies
themselves don't have an incentive to, or maybe
don't realize that this is a new product offering
they could expand into. There's no research novelty, so this isn't a research problem,
and policy is going to be too slow. So I
have been proposing that we should have field strategy as
a new role where people come and actually solve this
problem. And I know it is all fine and good
to say, yes, propose a new role. I hope that
you are all skeptical of me right now at this moment.
This isn't a hypothetical. I have made three
entities exist in this rough order: of talking to
experts, identifying where there is a gap, picking the
person who I think is perfectly suited to fill
that gap, handing them the problem, telling them
about the solution direction. And I think for
these three, at least, I helped co-author their
proposals to get funding to solve these problems.
Each of them ended up getting — I think the
first check for each of them was over $1 million. And
in terms of counterfactual impact, Jason Gross was doing mech-interp research at MIRI.
There were formal methods flavors, but he is literally the best person.
I still believe that he was the best person
in the world at that time to found an
AI-first auto-formalization for cybersecurity entity. I imagine at this point many of you have
heard of Theorem. Oath Technologies is a focused
research organization that will be launching soon,
and happy to go into more of like what Oath
and Earendil are doing later, if that is of interest,
and/or what my role was. But it might be also
worth going into a bit of who am I that does
this random stuff. I am not an expert in AI.
My background is materials engineering. My PhD was in
experimental quantum optics. And I basically have had
one job wearing many hats at the
biggest blockchain company you've never heard of, where I
was the first PhD hire. I built out all
the research infrastructure, and so that was how
we structured our research programs, did hiring,
made research grants to external entities. I led a special projects team that included
David Dalrymple, davidad, working on what is now what became Safeguarded AI. I was
in charge of the meta-science team of how
you use scientific processes to improve science as
a system. And we had an internship program one summer that included Dwarkesh Patel.
I ran a venture studio that spun out five companies
to build mechanisms for various aspects of making
it easier to fund public goods and commons.
And then davidad and Critch sat me down and I
said, this seems like — this AI stuff seems
important. If you think I can contribute, let me
know. I will quit and help with this. And
they gave me enough of an endorsement and urging
that I started Atlas Computing in summer of 2023.
Most of what we've been doing until now was building tooling for formal methods.
The field strategy stuff, those three entities that
were started, those were all on the side.
That was not my main job. It is becoming my main job.
I am now building out a team to do this. The
goal of this talk is to talk through
why some of these problems are systematically orphaned
and why you should care about these, why these may
not sound critical, but I would argue they are.
I'll talk through two examples of field strategy, maybe just one depending on time.
I'm hoping to have a bunch of time at
the end for discussion. We could even whiteboard out,
if someone cares about a risk that they
think is neglected, how would I apply field strategy
to that problem? We can roll over a whiteboard or
something. And then the two concrete asks on the
final slide, because I am, in fact, scaling this. One
of the reasons I would argue that there are
overlooked problems is the law of the instrument.
To VCs or startup founders, they assume
there is a product that could solve this. And some
of that may or may not be the case.
Researchers will also assume that every problem would
benefit from research, or the problems that
they are best equipped to solve are going to
be filtered through this process of, can I apply
my tools to this? How could I make this
better? This holds for traditional funders who issue RFPs,
and then all of the applications they receive
for their RFP are someone's passion project
under a coat of the topic of the RFP.
Having been a research funder, I speak from experience.
And this holds for policymakers and standards bodies as well.
This is the law of the instrument. To a man
with a hammer, everything looks like a nail. So you
should expect that in equilibrium, the problems —
and I'll acknowledge we are definitely far from
equilibrium — but in equilibrium, in a world like
this, if most people are looking at problems that
have certain properties, the problems that persist are
problems that cannot be solved by solutions
with those properties. I will also note that focused research organizations are another one
of these types of entities meant to fill
a gap. Atlas Computing is a Convergent Research project,
and you can ask me about FROs after, if
you are interested in that, what they are, etc.
I will also claim that the survivorship bias holds
for skill sets as well, for an individual. And
people who see a neglected, important, and tractable
risk will often think, I will use my
very particular set of skills for this. And the
problem with that is that it is rare that
the person who finds out about this does have the
perfect set of skills to do this. Most kidnapping
victims are not the children of spies. There's
also the "my normal approach is useless here."
I will, like, I will become an expert in
this. I will become an expert in something else.
And there's a risk of dramatically underestimating how hard that
is. I did try to find a tweet that
I remember Elon Musk reposting years ago, and I
failed to do it, but it was basically saying,
the first step of solving any significant problem
is dramatically underestimating how hard it is.
And I totally hold that is true. And
I totally think that you can have generalists
go and solve those things. But the thing the generalist brings, in my opinion,
is the ability to deal with uncertainty and pursue an important goal that,
through a changing environment, when it is not clear what solved looks like,
they just know directionally what the problem is.
And so I have been trying to figure out
what the best process looks like for an
alternative to this. We have outlined it here.
The first step is to start from, well,
AI systems should probably be able to do
some of these specific things that will cause
some risks to society. What would defensive
equilibria look like that we could move society into in preparation for those risks?
So that if that capability showed up, we
wouldn't be worried about that capability anymore.
And so I'll go into that, and then afterward go
into a bit of, for each of those equilibria,
what is an intervention that we could take,
and then de-risking that? And what does de-risking actually look like? And how does
that compare to the way other people use the
term field strategy? And then why handoff is relevant.
If you wanted to do this, I would say start
from a victory condition. What would you want the world
to look like? If you don't have that, there
are so many normative or value-based assumptions that one
might have to make in order to sketch out what
you should do. For those who are interested in
the philosophy side of that, Hume's guillotine or
the is-ought chasm is something that's worth
doing a bit of reading on. The method
that I advocate for is the tiling tree method,
popularized by an MIT neuro professor and the
founder of Convergent Research. The example in
this blog post is, let's start with, how would
you record the neural activity of a whole brain
at a single-cell resolution? Very hard problem. But you could theoretically say
there are criteria that would have to be true.
We could split this problem space into things that
are mutually exclusive and completely exhaustive, at every
level of a tree. MECE is this concept
from management consulting that is like, you can cover
a space and say, well, either it's going to
be — the recording will be digital or
analog. And because this is never digital and digital,
you know that that covers the space. And you can
keep doing this until you break this down into a
set of ideas. And the goal for this is not
to be comprehensive. The goal is to surface something
that is viable. And I think that that's a
very reasonable critique of, well, anytime you apply an
ontology, you're going to be wrong. And the goal is
not to be right. The goal is to try and get
inspiration to find more things. Because if you
go back to this again, your goal for identifying
defensive equilibria is to have enough that you can
find one that's viable. And so you could ask,
great, I don't care about neurons. I care
about that AI systems should follow human instructions
and not cause civilizational, societal collapse. And I
did a rough version of this, where you first
figure out, is it following anyone's instructions? Whose instructions are taking precedence? How
are you deciding that? Is the user using this
for intentional harm? How do you prevent that? And/or
are they causing indirect harm? How would you
prevent that? There are many ways you could
break this down. I tried to break it down
so that the green boxes were roughly what subsets
of the economy would you be modeling? Because
I think it's easier to deterministically forecast
subsets of an economy rather than, for instance, all
the people in a location, or all the people
with a particular skill set, or the hardware,
like the data center and its supply chain or
something like that. I will note that in
terms of doing this kind of decomposition, there's a
great [Andrew Snyder Beatie]'s four pillars for bio
that does a really great version of this.
And whether or not he would agree that this is
what he is doing, I think that it's a good
characterization. I can point to a bad version
that I did for cybersecurity in an evening.
And you can split it into hardware and software and
people. And you ideally want the system to do
only and exactly what it is told to do, what
you think it should do. I think that this needs work,
but you can use this to surface a bunch
of things that are like, here are some specific
things that should be done. What would it
take to, for instance, make tamper security
trustworthy, or have formal verification that was very
easy to apply to a lot of different things?
And once you go through this exercise, if there's interest,
I can share links for — I think I have,
at this point, over 100 different scoped projects that match
to one of these boxes. I also have one
of these for epistemic security and could cover, talk
about that too. But once you have a list,
there's a question of what do you do with
it? And there is a very clear pattern that
you can recognize in the AI safety and
AI security space of, great, let's ask experts
for neglected problems. Let's identify founders or general managers who can own those problems,
and then we will have impact because the founders will
solve the problem. And I don't want this to
sound like a critique because it's definitely not.
The Peregrine Report is an example of doing this.
They made it partway into step two before
realizing, hey, we should actually — this
is useful enough, we should just write up all
of this stuff. And have, I think, yeah, 208
expert proposals for reducing risk. I will note,
I have done something very similar to this.
I interviewed a lot of experts. I've interviewed
also people from the defense community or
intelligence community. And I can tell you, people get very excited about proposing ideas
that are well outside their skill set. And a
lot of those ideas are unfortunately really bad ideas.
You can take that and bring it to someone who
is an expert in those things and ask, hey,
would this work? And the answer is almost certainly no.
But the interesting thing is that you can
ask, how would you change this idea to make
it something that would work? If you shared the
assumptions that I have and the concerns I have,
what would you do on this? And it's a really
good way to extract expertise and the world models
that these individuals have about how the domain of their expertise is useful.
And so rather than looking at just these,
I would highlight that there are some other
steps that basically no one does. One of them is, when you have
a list of good neglected problems, scope those
down to identify very high-leverage things that
you can do rather than jump straight to
the, "it would be really great if."
You can de-risk this with technical experts and
say, hey, is this possible? Who would
have to say yes, this is possible, before a skeptical grantmaker would agree
that this is something that is worth funding? You can
also ask, who would have to adopt this before
it would actually be useful? To the extent
that humans are still the meaningful decision makers,
some human will have to do one thing versus
another for there to be impact of some work.
And you can also start identifying what are
the relevant skills, because "generalist founder or
general manager" is not a job description. You
can write a job description for these things,
and that will help you unearth who could
become that founder or general manager. And then you
can figure out why that person specifically, or
someone of that archetype, might say no to this,
and figure out what it would take for them
to say yes. That's roughly this portion — or,
sorry, no, that covers roughly to here, some of
the staffing. I will talk through one, if there
is interest, talk through two, because I'm going
pretty fast — two different examples of this.
The first one being that some people are
worried that there is no oversight on
model specs or the constitutions. And there is not really coordination. There's no loop
back to get — no accountability. It can
be changed. This could cause some concerns,
for instance, from a government official who wants it to read differently. And
if you don't have some sort of control
mechanism or governance structure, it becomes very brittle
to changes. And so you could start from
that and say, let's identify some defensive equilibria.
I think that the status quo of each lab running
on their own is not really a robust one.
You could imagine that a government body started
doing coordination or mandating some aspects of
these specifications. I think government doesn't move fast enough. You could imagine an industry
body housing it, or something that looks more co-authored, something collaborative
between the labs themselves. And if you were
to pick this last one, then the question becomes,
how would you go about actually manifesting that? You
need to know what good would look like there,
but also it is usually not something — these aren't
things you can jump from A to Z on. And
so the question becomes, what does B look
like? And you can identify some potential interventions.
Is there a narrow pain point that we
could solve related to mental health risks, or cybersecurity
risks, or concentration of power concerns? Is there something where setting up this entity
actually makes life better for the frontier — the participants you would need,
in this case, the frontier labs, based on
what the defensive equilibrium was? You could say,
you want to be able to come to them with,
let me solve this problem for you, not, please would you
do this, because it would be good. I think that
you can always tack on to the first one
"and it would be good," but getting to "this
will solve a problem for you," I think, should
be modeled as opening a lot more doors. The next
step would be drafting a Google Doc that can be
socialized with the relevant people and say, hey,
if you're worried about concentration of power,
this is a thing. If you're worried about
government intervention, to say, this is the
way we are going to add things to
the model spec to make sure that ChatGPT-6 is
highly aligned with US government interests. Ask them, if you were worried about this,
what would you do? Is this a direction
that would solve a problem for you potentially?
How would you change it to make this
useful, palatable, adoptable? And iterate on that. You
can ask also experts who have set up
governance bodies like this. You could ask antitrust counsel,
why would the most scrutinized companies reject this?
Can you change this so that it
would be more viable? Can you make this look
like a PR win for the labs that participate,
to add a carrot to the stick? I would say that in
a lot of strategic work, it is very easy to fall
into what is called hope chess in the chess
world, where you are assuming or expecting that your
opponent will not play optimally, or that things will
happen to work out based on your plan. And
I think it is much easier to succeed if
you are modeling everyone as capable people who are
appropriately overwhelmed by information, constrained by incentives, and things like this.
At the end of — another thing to
do is map out who would have to say
yes to this for it to work. And
if you can get conditional commitments from everyone, I would say that this becomes
the best possible artifact you could have at the penultimate step of field strategy.
You want frontier labs saying, yes, if this
legal entity existed and there were a person
who matches this profile, if that person were
signed on, we would be able to join.
And if you can get that commitment, even for some
very small thing, you can build off of that. And
you want to get that for as many, like, all
of the stakeholders. I think that the notion of an
adoption quorum will be relevant, better fleshed out
in the second example. But there is a sense
in which the conditional commitments solve the bootstrapping problem, because you can also get
that from the possible founder — you would get to
lead this, which is step four, which I will cover
after the second example, because it's the same
for both. That's what I wanted to cover there.
The second example could be something like, we
would want to be able to verify that
a data center is only — that we could in
the future want to verify that data center is
only being used for inference or only being
used for alignment research. And there are choices
around policy choices, for instance, that would be
dependent on how costly that is perceived to be.
If this looks like it would require years
to set up and would not be very reliable,
that might be something that doesn't happen. If this
is viewed as something that could be, at this
point, a software update and be doable within a week,
that seems like it would be much more likely
for the human decision maker to say, oh yeah,
okay, let's actually try to enforce this. And so
the question becomes, how would you have an
equilibrium where it becomes very easy to choose
to require restrictions on how much compute is
being used for things other than inference?
And you could break this down roughly into,
well, people check the machines directly, people check
the machines with existing trusted machines, which would be like satellite or telemetry directions,
or people build new trusted machines and put
them into the data centers. And I think that
the last one is by far the most reliable —
is really the only thing that would meet the
level of security requirements. There might be other defensive equilibria here that are worth
digging into. I would love to hear what they are.
But if you started with that last one of, great,
let's look at workload attestation on-chip — let's
assume that there's some kind of thing you could
leverage to get cryptographic attestations that this exists — does this look like
we're trying to update the hardware itself and
get NVIDIA to change what they're doing?
There are people at OpenAI who could make asks
of NVIDIA to change the hardware they are deploying
if it has certain criteria. What are those
criteria? I don't actually know what those
criteria are, but I have a sense of the
rough boundary, and a field strategist should be trying
to figure that out. There's also questions of, can
you bolt on new hardware? Could you add something
like a verifiable network monitor to check these
things that were tamper-proof? And then there's
a question of, should we just try and do the
best we can with software? And I would say that
I've spent a decent amount of time thinking
about specifically the first option. I have been
increasingly talking to people about the other two as
well. But if we dig into the first one,
you could see something like three relevant ways
that might get adopted. One of them is
there are actual economic incentives that, for instance, data center providers have for
providing the kind of security guarantees that would
be exactly what you would want for
verifiable monitoring. This would look like formally verified isolation of processes, so that
on the finance side, you know that your agents can't modify the billing.
But on the verification side, you would have — so
that you know that the agents or the other
applications can't modify what they are seeing in terms of monitoring various agent processes.
That is very separate from the adoption path
of a government requirement. If you could get something
that looked like signaling of a government requirement, then you could possibly get
meaningful changes to hardware. But that is a
very different incentive problem, a very different
adoption quorum. And the last one would be,
that I've identified, would be frontier labs saying
that they want to adopt this, they will require
this of their inference data centers so that they
can coordinate with each other in a trustworthy
fashion. Any one of these quorums is needed. It's
not clear to me which is the closest to yes.
And so trying to figure that out is something that is
necessary to get adoption, and also something that
is very hard for the models to do today.
And so a significant amount of the actual human labor of field strategy is,
first — small part — use the AIs to
identify these and identify the people and what their
incentives might be, and then go talk to
those people about what their incentives actually are,
or hire people as field strategists who have
been in those areas, who know what their
incentives actually are and can model them well,
or get them on the phone very quickly.
The other half of this is the technical de-risking
half, which might also look like a Google Doc
that you socialize with various people. In this
case, this is for an advanced market commitment
for formally verified AI containment for cloud infra providers, starting at the hypervisor and
verifying all the way down to the gates, and
saying there should be a tool that has these
properties, and if it had these properties, we
would pay this much for it. That's the advanced
market commitment side. I have actually gotten positive feedback from a distinguished engineer
on the security side at GCP and a relevant VP
at AWS saying, yes, this is a good idea,
there should be something like this. Currently in
the process of tracking down the relevant person
at Azure. The goal would be to put them all
in a room and say, can we agree on something? Can
we use philanthropic funding to incentivize or to subsidize the existence of this tool?
Because there are enough startups out there that
would build this, and enough contractors who would
build this tool if they knew exactly what it took
to get adoption by CSPs, that it feels like having
this coordination problem solved of what needs to
be done, what is the product requirements doc
for this thing that does not yet exist,
that being able to have this to coordinate around
seems like a meaningfully missing part. The last
step is to go and staff this problem.
I claim that field strategists are different from
founders meaningfully, in that they will hand off
— they will do much of this strategy that makes
it easier to find a founder, makes it easier for
a founder to start and succeed, and then hands it
off and does this again, because this is a skill.
When you're trying to staff the problem, you
should ask what skills are needed and
write the job description. You should figure out what the day-to-day work of
the person doing this thing looks like, and then go
find out who in the world has a job
where their day-to-day looks basically the same. This
is one of the most interesting learnings
from Convergent Research. The focused research organizations — there's, like,
12 that have been started — and for almost all
of them, I think it's about 20% people who are
like visionaries and 80% people who have been
doing almost exactly the same thing for the
last 10 to 20 years of their career, and are
now doing it in a meaningful — in a different context
towards a new end. But the work itself
looks very much the same. Their expertise, as, like,
a scientific high-vac — like hard vacuum technician — engineer, is like
the only thing that is relevant, and you need that
expertise to just import. And I will claim that if
there is something a person can do, there's almost
certainly someone in the world — I will claim
it is probably easy — I'm sorry, trying to
remove the qualifiers and they just come so naturally.
I think anything a person can do, someone out
in the world is getting paid to do professionally.
The world is big and weird, and there will be
someone who is getting paid to do that thing.
And the goal becomes, find that person, find
the best person there, find out why they aren't
working on this problem and why they wouldn't say yes
if you gave them all of the progress you have.
I would say the founder role is daunting in ways
that being able to take on this thing that a field
strategist has really evolved and gotten all of
these conditional commitments on is not. And
I think that it is very compelling to be on
the other end of a call where someone says,
somehow without your knowledge, you have become the perfect person to run this effort.
Do you want to do it? I can give you
all of these things, but I cannot do this work
myself because I do not have this expertise. You
are one of four people in the world who
seems to have the relevant expertise, and you
are the first person I'm talking to.
I will claim that I am deeply skeptical of anyone
who comes with a panacea and claims to be able to
solve all problems. There are obvious limitations to
this. The first one being, if you don't know
what good looks like, this does not work.
So specifically, if there's a ton of uncertainty,
like alignment research, I don't know what good
looks like. I don't know what done looks like.
I can't run this process on this. If
you have something that is more deterministic, or where
it is very costly to do this iteration, it
is very hard, if possible at all. And also
there are instances where I think you do
need a unicorn generalist founder who may not exist.
Just because this is a way of identifying possible
ways to solve a problem also doesn't mean that
there is a possible way to solve the problem, which
I think is a corollary to — there's no
rule that says we make it. But there
are also some nice properties of this process.
Specifically, that these interventions become by construction the best intervention, the best ways
we have come across as a field strategy
organization to solve this problem. If at any
point an expert had said, "that's dumb, you
should be doing this instead," the obvious response is,
well, if you had these constraints and this
goal and these assumptions, how would you solve it?
And then make them solve — make them basically do
your job for you — and they will be proud to
inform, they'll be proud to disabuse you of
your ignorance, and maybe they'll want to continue
doing so. And eventually you may have someone
who feels an unreasonable — not unreasonable,
a justified and large amount of ownership over
the solution that has been designed. And people often
have the concern of, well, great founders don't want
to be handed the solution — they want to
have some sense of ownership over developing that
solution. It turns out that if you've been
chatting with the same person for three months
as you've been scoping this and de-risking it,
they will probably have a lot of ownership
over that solution direction. And if you ask them,
actually, hey, what would it take for you to say
yes to running this? Would you — is there
an amount of money or support or ownership
or de-risking that would make this something that you
said, yeah, I will leave this job, I will leave
my current job to do this because it's gotten
over the line? Where is that line? Worst-case
scenario, they will tell you there isn't one,
but usually putting them in the mindset of solving
this as a problem ends up making them negotiate
against their status quo in favor of changing.
So lots of framing-type questions like this.
There's also a nice feature where picking the cause area,
and scoping the interventions, and executing are separated, which means you get
